# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

insights.line: What made the others more pressing?

whys.g1: Lena and Aisha both say safety and insurance beat yield, which is one plain group, while my point about getting cash back fast to pay bills and Rachel's about runway and her accountant's tax advice are different reasons that don't fit there or with each other.

screens.why2: Runway, the insured limit, getting cash back and moving money between accounts are plain finance-lead words, and every row reads on first pass.
screens.why3: Every row is something a finance lead at a funded startup does with the raise cash, so it is answerable from their own month.
screens.why4: The four rivals are distinct, but 'Choosing where the raise cash sits' is so broad it holds 'keeping cash safe' and 'getting cash back fast', since those are reasons for choosing where it sits.
screens.why5: My problem is earning more on cash the company will not touch for months without risking it or switching banks; 'choosing where the raise cash sits' drops the earning and keeps only the circumstance.
screens.why7: The own row is first, locked and present with four rivals, so the belief can go either way, but it restates the circumstance ('decides where cash from a raise sits'), which the card forbids; that makes the belief near-circular and the row a parent of two rivals.
screens.instead: Own row 'Earning more on cash not needed for months' first, then Knowing the months of runway left · Keeping cash safe above the insured limit · Getting cash back fast when needed · Moving money between accounts without mistakes

screens.why1: Right after the hard parts of the cash decision, it is natural to ask how finance leads park the raise money today and how well that goes, and this is the last of the four Problem screens.
screens.why2: The question says 'until the company sends it' where my job reads 'spends it', so I had to read it twice, and the job pasted whole into the question makes it long; the hint ('checking for errors by hand') is also far from a treasury move.
screens.why3: Where the raise money sits and what it earns after fees is exactly what a startup finance lead sees on the treasury dashboard every month.
screens.why4: My two boxes hold the act and its means (bank treasury money market fund at about 3.5% after fees) and four distinct rungs from market rate down to next to nothing, and 'Leave this out of the study' is the right founder-side escape.
screens.why5: My boxes are kept word for word, but the question turns my job's 'spends it' into 'sends it', a small drift in my own words.
screens.why7: Every rung is on one measure (what the cash earned after fees, the money cost my Answer names), the first rung 'Earned a market rate after fees' is today's way working, the rest step down without overlap toward 'next to nothing' and leave Keel room for a fifth failing rung, so the belief can be both supported and refuted, and the founder escape is there.
screens.instead: How do finance leads keep money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it? (e.g. 'parking the reserve in the bank's treasury fund')

screens.why1: After I said how finance leads keep raise cash today, checking the five ways that goes is the obvious next step before the problem is tested.
screens.why2: 'Market rate after fees' is how a startup finance lead talks about the reserve's yield, so every rung reads on first pass.
screens.why3: A finance lead sees the treasury rate and the fee on the Mercury or Brex dashboard every month, so they know roughly where they landed.
screens.why4: The rungs are distinct and in our words, but 'a bit under' and 'well under' market have no number, so they blur; there is also no rung for actually losing principal, which happened to the startup in a short-term bond fund that lost 9% in 2022.
screens.why5: These are my own four rungs as I reworded them, and the belief names the bank's treasury product exactly as I mean it.
screens.why7: One measure (rate after fees), five rungs best to worst, a working first rung and the line under rung 2 all meet the card; but the last rung, 'The cash sat in checking', is a different act from 'keeping the money in the bank's treasury product' rather than that act failing outright.
screens.instead: Earned a market rate after fees · Earned a bit under market after fees · ┄ line ┄ · Earned well under market after fees · Earned next to nothing after fees · Lost money on the reserve

screens.why1: Choosing who reads my questions to finance leads belongs here, just before the study goes out, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: It is plain on first read: two interviewers, a 5-second preview of each, one price of 400 credits whichever I pick, and the link sent by text.
screens.why3: Picking the voice my finance-lead respondents will hear is my own call, and I can decide it by listening to the two previews.
screens.why4: The two options are distinct and each has a preview, but they are bare names; the hint says the interview is on video yet only voices are offered, so I cannot tell whether I am also picking a face or what differs besides the sound.
screens.why5: It keeps 'finance leads' as I typed it and shows respondents nothing of Palus or my roles.
screens.instead: Who should ask finance leads your questions on video? (Daphne, warm US voice and face ▶ 5 s · Saskia, brisk US voice and face ▶ 5 s), with one line saying the face and voice come together.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, it is obvious I next pick how finance leads will answer the link I send them.
screens.why2: AI interviewer on video, read and tap, or let them choose are plain to a founder who builds software for startups; 'Daphne' is named and explained in the same line.
screens.why3: I know my batchmates and their finance leads: busy people who would rather tap through a form than sit on a video call, so I can pick from what I know.
screens.why4: The three options are complete and distinct (video AI, text, or both), each described in plain words, and my pick 'Read and tap' is there.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is changed or leaked; the screen is only about format and names finance leads as I typed them.

screens.why1: Once the interviews are set up, choosing who gets a link is the obvious last step before sending, and I'd send to batchmates I know by name.
screens.why2: The three options are written in plain founder words (people I know, a list from search, one open link in a group), and I'd pick on first read.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I'd reach: finance leads and ops people at batchmate startups I can name one by one.
screens.why4: Named people, a sourced list and an open group link cover the real ways I'd reach finance leads, they don't overlap, and none is missing.
screens.why5: My pick, each person by name, is kept as typed, and nothing about Palus leaks into the choice.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' is stated, but the number beside it is Frequency's median of 2 months out of 3, which sits inside my own 2-to-3 band, so it does not show why the stage split; Importance at 3 of 7 (2 short) is the card that hurts most and it is not the one named.
screens.why_b2: The tally (1 holding, 3 split, 7 answered) and each card's 'bar 5 of 7, N short' read at once, but Frequency's line puts 'median 2 months' next to '3 of 7 below what you said' and I had to read it twice to see the median is in my band while the count still falls short, and 'among these 7 7 of 7' has a doubled 7.
screens.why_b3: The four dimensions and the Importance and Current solution lines are mine, but Prevalence and Frequency say finance leads 'move raise cash into the bank's default treasury product' each month, when my belief is that the reserve sits there and the monthly move is the transfer back out to checking.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page tells me what a split on Importance and Current solution means for Palus. The only text under the title restates the problem I typed in.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is in the kicker and on every card, Prevalence is hedged 'among these 7', and the three splits are called splits, not support.
screens.instead: Lead with Importance: only 3 of 7 put where the reserve sits among their two hardest things, and 3 of 7 are content with the bank's treasury. The pain is real for some but not most, so find out what sets those 3 or 4 apart (balance size, a board cash policy) before pitching yield to everyone.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up above your band' sits beside the deciding number, 7 of 7 said yes against a bar of 5 of 7, although 'among these 7 7 of 7' runs together and needs a breath.
screens.why_b2: The strip counts seven gate answers, all for me, on a 0-to-7 axis, and the marker at 5 is labelled 'at least 6 in 10', so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence and 'moved raise cash into the bank's default treasury product' are my belief, but the line says plain 'finance leads' and drops my qualifier 'at startups holding cash from a raise'.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7' plus a pointer to the next two cards tells me where to look next, but not what a unanimous yes means for Palus, for instance that nearly every lead I'd reach is sitting in the bank product I want them to leave.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, 'a small group: a lean, not a call' says it plainly, and 'Common among these 7' claims nothing beyond the people who answered.
screens.instead: Holding up, above your band: all 7 finance leads at startups holding raise cash said yes, against a bar of 5 of 7. That is a small group, a lean. Nobody said no, so check Frequency and Importance to see whether being in the bank's product actually costs them.

screens.why_b1: People disagree sits right beside 4 of 7 at or beyond my 2 to 3 months, against a bar of 5 of 7, 1 short, so I know both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: Months out of 3 over 7 people with the bar at 5 reads quickly, but the axis starts at a 0 nobody could answer, and the legend's 'what you said' next to 'at what you said' took me a second look.
screens.why_b3: Frequency and 2 to 3 months out of 3 are mine, but the act reads as moving raise cash into the bank's treasury product, when the monthly move I meant is pulling cash out to cover burn, and the asked line says the month twice and trails off with 'the most recent time it happened'.
screens.why_b4: It tells me I am 1 short of the bar and to read the next card, but not what a once-a-month-or-less move means for selling a set-up-once rule.
screens.why_b5: 7 answered and 7 counted stays visible, and the small group is called a lean, not a call, so nothing claims more than the people who answered.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 moved raise cash on 2 or 3 of the last 3 months, 1 short of the 5 you needed; 3 did it once, so for many the monthly transfer is rarer than you think. See Importance next.

screens.why_b1: The status 'People disagree' sits right beside '3 of 7 put it in their two · bar 5 of 7 · 2 short', so I can see at once that my belief fell two people short of the bar I set.
screens.why_b2: The caption says what the bars count (picks, 14 from 7 people choosing two each), the bars add up to 14, and the strip puts the marker at 5 of 7, so I can read what is counted, over whom and where the bar is at first look.
screens.why_b3: 'Choosing where the raise cash sits' only restates my circumstance and loses what I was selling, earning more on cash I won't touch for months without risking it, and 'last months after a raise' is not how I would name the moment, though I can still tell it is my belief.
screens.why_b4: The So line says I tie with runway, safety above the insured limit and getting cash back fast, but it never says what that means for Palus, for example that buyers see yield as no more pressing than liquidity and safety and so I should lead with those.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is shown and labelled 'a lean, not a call', the tie is stated accurately at 3 picks each, and nothing claims more than 3 of 7 can support (only 'ranked others first' is a little loose, since they picked rather than ranked).
screens.instead: 3 of 7 put earning more on idle raise cash in their two, short of your 5; it is level with knowing runway, keeping cash safe above the insured limit and getting it back fast, so lead with safety and next-day access, not the extra yield.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' sits right beside its number: 4 of 7 said today's way falls short against a bar of 5 of 7, 1 short.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the seven answers by rung, marks my line between 'a bit under market' and 'well under market', and the strip puts the marker at 5 of 7, so all three read on first look.
screens.why_b3: The belief names my act in my words: keeping the raise money in the bank's treasury product, for finance leads, still falling short.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the count and then sends me to the Insights tab; it never says what 3 of 7 settling for a bit under market means for my pitch, which is that yield alone won't move them unless switching is nearly effortless.
screens.why_b5: The screen does say n is small ('a lean, not a call'), but calling the three who earned a bit under market 'content' claims more than the rung says, since one of them is the person who won't 'bet the company' on yield.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 fell short, 1 short of the bar on a small group. The 3 who earned a bit under market accepted the gap rather than lose safety or add work, so test whether a no-switch, low-effort setup changes that.

screens.why_b1: Both boxes open on 'People disagree' with the deciding count right beside it (3 of 7 against a bar of 5, 2 short; 4 of 7 against a bar of 5, 1 short), so I know each line missed and by how much.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are my dimensions, and the belief lines (choosing where the raise cash sits as one of their top two, the bank's treasury product falling short) are the beliefs I checked.
screens.why_b4: Under 'When a line fails' there is no line on what the misses mean for Palus, such as leading with insurance and same-day access ahead of yield, so I have to work out the next step myself.
screens.why_b5: Every group carries its count, the 4 of 4 asked is shown, and the empty Current solution box says plainly that no one was asked and names the three who never saw it, so nothing claims more than the answers hold.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add what I never typed: a board after the bank failures asks only whether the money is insured, an accountant wants plain cash for the tax break, and monthly bill-paying out of treasury makes two-click access beat another point of yield.
screens.instead: Say what to do next: safety above the insured limit and fast access beat yield for 4 of 7, so lead with custody, insurance and 1-2 day liquidity before the rate; and on Current solution, say why no one was asked here instead of leaving an empty question.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it's an obvious gate: it checks that I run a startup's money at a Mercury or Brex style bank before asking anything else.
screens.why2: I know Mercury and Brex well, but "a similar provider" made me pause, because we also hold money at a big bank and a treasury account, and I'm not sure whether those count.
screens.why3: I know where our accounts are without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct for a gate, and §5 says a gate gets no escape.
screens.why5: It names the founder's segment in plain trade terms and shows nothing of the product or roles.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two options that are easy to hear and answer.
screens.instead: Does your startup keep its operating cash with Mercury, Brex or another startup-focused bank? Yes / No

screens.why1: Right after confirming we bank with Mercury, asking whether I put raise money into the bank's own treasury option is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: I'd say 'cash from our raise' and 'Mercury Treasury', not 'raise cash'; 'default treasury product' needs a second read to work out whether it means the bank's own sweep or something I picked by default.
screens.why3: I run our accounts, so I know exactly where the money sits and whether I moved any of it in the last three months.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it and don't overlap; the chips belong to the story box, not the gate.
screens.why5: 'Default' carries someone else's judgement that the bank's treasury is the lazy, unexamined choice, when for us it's a deliberate pick because the operational burden matters more than a bit more yield.
screens.why6: Short, one question, 'Yes or no' is easy to hold, though 'raise cash' runs together a little when heard.
screens.why7: Yes and No are both true of someone, but the stem asks a routine move rather than the cost, and someone whose raise cash already sat there before the window has to say No even if they have the problem, so the gate bends the one-act-that-hurts rule.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did you put cash from your raise into your bank's own treasury account? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to moving raise money into the bank's treasury product, asking how often I did it follows naturally.
screens.why2: I'd say 'cash from the round' and 'Mercury Treasury' or 'the money market sweep'; 'raise cash' and 'the bank's default treasury product' take a second read, and 'months' is said twice.
screens.why3: I made these transfers myself, so I know which months I moved money, like the $300k transfer.
screens.why4: The buttons 1, 2 and 3 cover every month of the window without overlap, and 'I can't recall' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: 'Default treasury product' sounds like someone's product framing rather than how I talk about my bank's sweep, so it drifts a little toward the founder's terms.
screens.why6: It is short and is one question, and 'a number from 1 to 3, or say you can't recall' is easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: The measure, the 1-to-3 buttons and the escape all meet the card, but the window's unit is said twice ('in the last 3 months, in how many months'), which is a listed pitfall, so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, on how many months did you move cash from the round into your bank's treasury or money market account? 1 · 2 · 3 · I can't recall

screens.why1: After asking whether and how often I moved raise cash into the bank's treasury product, asking which part of handling that cash I'd most like made easier is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: The options are my words (insured limit, runway, moving money between accounts), but 'your last months after a raise' is an odd anchor I'd have to read twice, since a raise isn't a monthly occasion and I'd wonder which months it means.
screens.why3: These are all things I do myself: sweeping cash above the FDIC limit, picking where it sits, wiring between Mercury accounts, pulling cash back for payroll, and tracking runway.
screens.why4: 'Choosing where the raise cash sits' swallows two other rows, because keeping it safe above the insured limit and getting it back fast are the things I weigh when I choose where it sits, so they overlap; the escape fits.
screens.why5: Nothing about the product leaks to me, but the row that looks like the founder's reads like the situation said again rather than a difficulty, and the 'earning' half of the job is gone from every option.
screens.why6: The five options are short and easy to hold when heard, but 'Think of your last months after a raise' is clumsy spoken aloud.
screens.why7: The own row is on the list, not first, with the right escape and enough other rows to fill both picks, but it restates the circumstance and two rivals are parts of it, which bends the card's no-overlap and own-item rules.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you decided where to put cash from a raise. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Comparing where to put the cash · Keeping cash above the insured limit safe · Getting cash back in time for spending · Moving money between accounts without mistakes · Knowing how many months of runway are left · None of these

screens.why1: Asking why I put getting money out and moving it around ahead of picking where it sits follows straight from the last screen and is the natural thing to ask next.
screens.why2: It pastes the long row back at me, two things joined by 'and' and called 'those' though I picked one, and 'choosing where cash sits' isn't how I'd say it; I'd say 'where we park the cash' or 'chasing yield'.
screens.why3: I know exactly why: the operational burden of getting cash out of treasury and between accounts matters more to us than a bit more yield.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: 'Choosing where cash sits' is someone's framing word for word rather than mine, so the comparison drifts toward the study's own terms.
screens.why6: It is one question, but the pasted-back clause with two picks against a third is a mouthful to hold before the 'why' arrives.
screens.instead: You said getting cash out quickly mattered most, more than where you park it. Why is that?

screens.why1: After asking whether and how often I moved raise cash into Mercury's treasury, asking how that has gone is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: 'Think of your last cash balance' makes me stop, because I look at the balance every day and it isn't an occasion; 'the last month-end' or 'the last time I moved cash in' would be plain.
screens.why3: I know we earn about 3.2%, but whether that is 'a bit under' or 'well under' market depends on which market rate you mean, so I'd be guessing at the rung.
screens.why4: 'A bit under' and 'well under' have no edge between them, and the last option, cash sitting in checking, isn't a way keeping it in the treasury product went, so it answers a different question than the stem asks.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product leaks, but 'the bank's default treasury product' is someone else's phrase; I'd say 'Mercury Treasury' or 'the sweep'.
screens.why6: Short stem and five short parallel options with one escape at the end; 'after fees' four times is repetitive but easy to hold.
screens.why7: It has five rungs on one money measure, a working first rung and an escape, but the last rung leaves the act the stem names, so 'failed outright' is a different act, not the worst outcome of this one.
screens.instead: Think of the last month-end. How did the raise cash in Mercury Treasury do? Earned what we expected · Earned a little less than expected · Earned well under what we expected · Earned next to nothing · Never got moved out of checking; or say someone else handles it.

screens.why1: I just said treasury works for us, so asking why is the natural next question and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: It reads back what I said in my words, but 'what keeps it working' is a bit off: nothing needs maintaining, it just runs, so I'd have to work out that they mean 'why do you stick with it'.
screens.why3: I know exactly why: it's built into the bank, it sweeps on its own, there's no extra account to manage, and that low operational burden matters more to us than squeezing out more yield than about 3.2%.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: Nothing of anyone's product or plan comes through; it's just about my own setup.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, one question, no symbols or asides, easy to answer after one hearing.
screens.instead: You said keeping the raise money in your bank's treasury works for you. What makes it worth staying with?
